paper_information.title: Handbook of Pigeonpea Diseases (Revised)
paper_information.journal_or_source: Information Bulletin No. 42 (Revised 2012), International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT)
paper_information.abstract_summary: Pigeonpea is an important grain legume in the semi-arid tropics. This bulletin provides information on causal agents, distribution, economic importance, symptoms, epidemiology, and management of major diseases of pigeonpea, supplemented with photographs, a diagnostic key, and control measures.
paper_information.research_objective: To assist in field diagnosis and management of major pigeonpea diseases through symptomatology, distribution, epidemiology, and control measures.
important_findings: More than 60 pathogens infect pigeonpea, but only a few cause major economic losses.
Sterility mosaic and witches' broom are region-specific, while Fusarium wilt and Phytophthora blight are widespread.
Providing diagnostic keys, resistant varieties, cultural practices, and chemical treatments aids effective disease management.

general: Seedling disease appearing within a month of sowing
Patches of dead seedlings at the primary leaf stage
Seedlings turn slightly chlorotic before dying
Rotting in the collar region covered with white mycelial growth
Seedlings uprooted easily with lower root remaining in soil
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of dead seedlings scattered over the field

field_identification: White or brown sclerotial bodies attached to the collar region or in the soil around dead seedlings
Rotting in collar region covered with white mycelial growth
differential_diagnosis: Differentiated from seedling diseases caused by Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or Pythium by white mycelial growth on the rotting collar region

causes_and_risk_factors: Undecomposed organic matter left on seedbeds
Pigeonpea following cereal crops like sorghum without clearing stubble

other_conditions: Early-sown (June) crops more affected than later-sown crops in India

severity_and_yield_loss: A minor disease that can cause severe losses when undecomposed organic matter is left on the surface of seedbeds

cultural_management: Deep summer ploughing
Select well drained fields
Keep the fields free from un-decomposed organic matter
Sow when soil moisture is low
Select fields where cereal crops (such as sorghum) have not been grown during the previous season
Collect cereal stubble from the field and destroy it before sowing pigeonpea

diseases.causal_agent: Phytophthora drechsleri Tucker f. sp. cajani

general: Resembles damping off disease causing seedlings to die suddenly
Water-soaked lesions on leaves
Brown to black, slightly sunken lesions on stems and petioles
Infected leaves lose turgidity and become desiccated
Lesions girdle main stems or branches causing them to break and foliage above to dry up
Production of large galls on stems especially at edges of lesions in plants not killed
Infects foliage and stems but not the root system
visual_field_symptoms: Leaves large gaps in plant stands
Appears first in low-lying areas of fields where water temporarily stagnates

field_identification: Water-soaked leaf lesions
Brown to black slightly sunken stem/petiole lesions
Stem breakage at infection point with stem galls

causes_and_risk_factors: Soilborne fungus surviving as chlamydospores, oospores, and dormant mycelium
Thick canopy of short-duration types and close spacing (30 x 10 cm)
Higher genetic susceptibility
Wild relative Cajanus scarabaeoides var. scarabaeoides is a host

favorable_conditions.humidity: Warm and humid weather following infection results in rapid development
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: More common on Alfisols than Vertisols; low-lying areas where water temporarily stagnates
other_conditions: Continuous leaf wetness for eight hours required for infection

disease_development_and_spread: Wind and rain help disseminate zoospores and facilitate infection through plant damage
epidemiology: Plants gradually develop tolerance as they grow older and are not infected after 60 days of age
severity_and_yield_loss: A devastating disease that kills young (1-7-week-old) plants
Yield losses usually higher in short duration pigeonpea than medium- and long-duration types

cultural_management: Early or normal sowing
Practice ridge planting methods
Summer solarization and summer ploughing should be done
Select fields with no previous record of blight
Avoid sowing pigeonpea in fields with low-lying patches that are prone to waterlogging
Prepare raised seed beds and provide good drainage
Use wide inter-row spacing

chemical_management.timing: Two sprays at 15-day intervals starting from 15 days after germination

general: Patches of dead plants in the field when flowering or podding
Purple band extending upwards from the base of the main stem (more easily seen in green stems)
Partial wilting of the plant (associated with lateral root infection), distinct from total wilt (tap root infection)
Browning of stem tissue in the region of the purple band
Browning or blackening of xylem when stem/primary branches are split open
Die-back symptoms on lower branches with purple band extending from tip downwards and internal xylem blackening
Leaf symptoms before death: loss of leaf turgidity, inter-veinal clearing, chlorosis to bright yellow leaves
early_symptoms: Sometimes occur earlier when plants are 1-2 months old (may lack purple band but show internal browning/blackening)
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of dead plants in the field during flowering or podding

field_identification: Purple band on main stem
Partial or total wilting
Browning/blackening of xylem upon splitting stems
differential_diagnosis: Distinguished from termite damage, drought, and Phytophthora blight (which kill the whole plant) by partial wilting

causes_and_risk_factors: Seed and soilborne fungus surviving on infected plant debris in soil for up to 10 years
Long- and medium-duration types suffer more than short-duration types
Ratooning predisposes plants to wilt

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: More severe on Vertisols than on Alfisols
other_conditions: Early sowing, good weed management, and good crop growth encourage wilt development
Pigeonpeas intercropped with sorghum are less attacked by wilt than sole-cropped plants

severity_and_yield_loss: Annual losses estimated at US$71 million in India and US$5 million in eastern Africa

cultural_management: Collect and burn plant residues after harvesting
Do summer ploughing
Select a field with no previous record of wilt for at least 3 years
Select seed from disease-free fields
Grow pigeonpea intercropped or mixed with cereal crops, eg, sorghum
Rotate pigeonpea with sorghum, tobacco, or castor every 3 years
Uproot wilted plants and use them for fuelwood
Solarize the field in summer to help reduce inoculum

diseases.causal_agent: Rhizoctonia bataticola (Taub.) Butler, Macrophomina phaseolina (Tassi) Goidanich

general: Infected plants suddenly and prematurely dry up
Rotten and shredded roots
Finer roots affected with dark, blackened streaks underneath bark with dark sclerotial bodies
Brittle roots that break when touched
Root rotting extends to base of stem under hot, humid conditions
Spindle-shaped lesions on stems and branches with light gray centers, brown margins, and scattered pycnidial bodies
Lesions coalesce causing branches or whole plants to dry up and die
visual_field_symptoms: Suddenly and prematurely dried up plants

field_identification: Rotten and shredded roots with dark sclerotial bodies
Spindle-shaped stem lesions with light gray centers

causes_and_risk_factors: Serious problem in late-sown or summer crops and in perennial or ratooned pigeonpeas
Affects short-duration pigeonpeas sown in rainy season
Crops more susceptible in reproductive stage than vegetative stage

favorable_conditions.humidity: Hot and dry weather encourage development; hot, humid conditions extend root rotting to stem base
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Rain after a prolonged dry spell predisposes plants to disease
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: More prevalent on Vertisols than on Alfisols

cultural_management: Disease incidence can be reduced if previous crop stubble is buried deep and allowed to decompose well before pigeonpea is sown
Select fields with no previous record of dry root rot
Avoid sowing late so that crop escapes drought and high temperatures at maturity

general: Normally seen at advanced stages of plant growth
Initial stem lesions with gray centers and dark brown margins containing pycnidia
Lesions coalesce and girdle the stem, developing into large swollen cankers leading to premature plant death
early_symptoms: Lesions on stems with gray centers and dark brown margins containing pycnidia
advanced_symptoms: Large swollen cankers girdling the stem leading to premature plant death
visual_field_symptoms: Large cankers on stem

field_identification: Large swollen cankers on stems with pycnidia

cultural_management: Avoid fields with previous records of the disease
Remove infected plants to reduce the build-up of inoculum in the soil

diseases.causal_agent: Colletotrichum cajani Rangel, Colletotrichum graminicola (Ces.) Wilson

general: Minor stem disease appearing as irregular brown to grayish stem lesions containing dark scattered acervuli
Severe infection leads to drying and death of infected branches
Minute spots with dark margins and gray centers scattered with acervuli common on leaves and pods
visual_field_symptoms: Irregular brown to grayish stem lesions with dark acervuli

field_identification: Stem lesions with dark acervuli
Minute spots with dark margins and gray centers on leaves and pods

cultural_management: Avoid fields with previous blight records

general: Sudden death of plants without external stem symptoms, but easily uprooted
Waterlogged roots are rotten, foul-smelling, bark easy to peel off
Brown patches with wavy margins in collar region (seen when bark is peeled off)
Reddish brown discontinuous streaks in the wood
visual_field_symptoms: Dead plants in field without external stem symptoms

field_identification: Brown patches with wavy margins in collar region
Reddish brown discontinuous streaks in wood
Rotten, foul-smelling roots with easily peeling bark
differential_diagnosis: Can be confused with wilt or Phytophthora blight, but distinguished by brown patches with wavy margins in collar region and reddish brown discontinuous streaks in wood
Reddish brown discontinuous streaks differ from wilt streaks (black and continuous)

causes_and_risk_factors: Highly susceptible to waterlogging
Adult pigeonpea plants more susceptible than seedlings
Pigeonpea suffers less damage in weedy or intercropped fields than well-weeded sole cropped fields

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Most severe when a few days of rain and cloudy weather are followed by sunny days

severity_and_yield_loss: Can result in sudden death of plants

diseases.disease_name: Bacterial Leaf Spot and Stem Canker
diseases.causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. cajani (Kulkarni, Patel & Abhyankar) Dye

general: Small necrotic spots surrounded by bright yellow halos on lower leaves (about 1 month old)
Rough, raised, cankerous lesions appear on the stem
Leaf spots do not usually cause defoliation
Cankers can cause stems to break, but broken part usually remains attached
Stem cankers increase in size up to 15-25 cm long
Severe infection causes affected branches to dry
early_symptoms: Small necrotic spots surrounded by bright yellow halos on lower leaves of ~1 month old plants
advanced_symptoms: Stem cankers increasing in size up to 15-25 cm long
Drying of affected branches in severe infections
visual_field_symptoms: Broken stems with cankerous lesions
Enlarged stem cankers

field_identification: Necrotic leaf spots with bright yellow halos
Raised cankerous stem lesions and broken stems

causes_and_risk_factors: African germplasm more susceptible than Indian germplasm
Pigeonpea with purple stems less susceptible to stem canker than those with green stems
Leaf infection at all stages, stem infection usually in younger plants

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Appears in India in rainy season (July and August)
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Incidence generally higher in low-lying waterlogged areas than well-drained areas

cultural_management: Select well-drained fields
Select seed from healthy crops

diseases.causal_agent: Oidiopsis taurica (Lev.) Salmon (Teleomorph: Leveillula taurica [Lev.] Arnaud)

general: White powdery fungal growths on aerial parts (leaves, flowers, pods)
Stunting of young plants followed by white powdery growth before flowering stage
Initial small chlorotic spots on upper leaf surface, followed by white powdery patches on corresponding lower surfaces
Powdery growth covers entire lower leaf surface upon sporulation
Severe infections result in heavy defoliation
early_symptoms: Small chlorotic spots on upper surface of individual leaves
advanced_symptoms: White powdery patches on lower surfaces covering the entire lower leaf surface
visual_field_symptoms: Defoliation in severely affected plants

field_identification: White powdery fungal growth on leaves, flowers, and pods
Chlorotic spots on upper leaf surface with powdery patches underneath

causes_and_risk_factors: Polycyclic disease (initial infection and secondary spread)
Infection directly proportional to conidia inoculum quantity
Indian varieties with thin, succulent leaves more susceptible than Kenyan varieties with thick leaves
Plants attacked by sterility mosaic or phyllody support abundant sporulation and act as continuous source of inoculum
Survives on perennial pigeonpeas, volunteer plants in shade, ratoon growth of stubbles, and as dormant mycelium on axillary buds
Early sowing and irrigation in India encourage establishment

favorable_conditions.humidity: Cool, humid climate congenial for infection/colonization; warm humid climate good for sporulation/spore dispersal

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas affected with the disease that are a source of inoculum
Sow late (after July) in India, to reduce disease incidence

diseases.causal_agent: Cercospora cajani Hennings (most prevalent), Cercospora indica Singh, Cercospora instabilis Rangel, Cercospora thirumalacharii Sharma & Mishra (Teleomorph: Mycovellosiella cajani [Henn.] Rangel ex Trotter)

general: Small circular to irregular necrotic spots or lesions usually on older leaves
Lesions coalesce causing leaf blight and defoliation
During epidemics, lesions appear on young branches causing tips to dry and die
Indian isolates produce fluffy mycelial growth on lesions, African isolates produce concentric zonations
early_symptoms: Small circular to irregular necrotic spots on older leaves
advanced_symptoms: Lesions coalesce causing leaf blight and defoliation
Drying of branch tips during epidemics
visual_field_symptoms: Small necrotic spots on older leaves
Concentric zonation on leaf

field_identification: Small necrotic spots on older leaves
Concentric zonations (African isolates) or fluffy mycelial growth (Indian isolates)

causes_and_risk_factors: More common in long-duration and perennial pigeonpeas grown in eastern Africa

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Cyclonic rains in southern and north-eastern peninsular India result in sudden outbreaks in certain years
other_conditions: Normally appears when plants are flowering and podding

severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses up to 85% reported from eastern Africa
Losses are severe when defoliation occurs before flowering and podding

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas that are a source of inoculum
Select seed from healthy crops

diseases.causal_agent: Alternaria sp, Alternaria tenuissima (Kunze ex Persoon) Wiltshire, Alternaria alternata (Fries) Keissler

general: Small, circular, necrotic spots on leaves that develop quickly forming typically concentric rings
Lesions appear on all aerial plant parts including flowers, flower buds, and pods
Blighting of leaves, severe defoliation, and drying of infected branches
early_symptoms: Small, circular, necrotic spots on leaves
advanced_symptoms: Concentric rings on spots, blighting of leaves, severe defoliation, and drying of infected branches
visual_field_symptoms: Necrotic spot on leaf
Drying of flowers and flower buds

field_identification: Circular necrotic spots with concentric rings on leaves and floral parts

causes_and_risk_factors: Emerging disease under climate change scenario
Not serious in rainy-season crops sown at normal time, but causes problems in crops sown late (September) or in postrainy season on plains of north-eastern India
Seed infection only reported from Puerto Rico

favorable_conditions.humidity: Warm, humid conditions favor fungal sporulation

cultural_management: Avoid fields close to perennial pigeonpeas
Select seed from healthy crops
Sow early

general: Round, necrotic spots up to 10 mm in diameter on leaves
Lesions have wavy dark brown margins with gray centers, containing characteristically concentric rings of pycnidial bodies
Severe infections result in desiccation and defoliation
early_symptoms: Round, necrotic spots up to 10 mm in diameter
advanced_symptoms: Concentric rings of pycnidial bodies, desiccation, and defoliation in severe infections
visual_field_symptoms: Necrotic leaf spots with pycnidial bodies

field_identification: Round necrotic leaf spots with wavy dark brown margins, gray centers, and concentric rings of pycnidia

favorable_conditions.humidity: Mean humidity range of 73-80% favors severe outbreaks
other_conditions: Problem in warm, humid climates; appears usually in July and persists throughout cropping season; serious epidemics in October in north-eastern plains of India

general: Problem on pigeonpea crops in north-eastern hills of India
Dark brown, circular to elliptical lesions (2-10 mm diameter) originating on leaf margins
Lesions coalesce to form dark brown patches
Infected leaves become yellow and dry prematurely
White mycelia with abundant conidia appear on blighted leaves under humid weather
early_symptoms: Dark brown, circular to elliptical lesions on leaf margins
advanced_symptoms: Coalescence into dark brown patches, premature yellowing and drying

field_identification: Dark brown circular/elliptical lesions on leaf margins coalescing into patches

favorable_conditions.humidity: Humid weather causes white mycelia and abundant conidia to appear

general: Dark brown raised pustules full of uredia on lower leaf surfaces
Infected leaves desiccate and drop off
Extensive defoliation when infections are severe
advanced_symptoms: Desiccation and dropping of leaves, extensive defoliation
visual_field_symptoms: Rust pustules on the lower leaf surface

field_identification: Dark brown raised pustules with uredia on lower leaf surfaces

favorable_conditions.rainfall: Light rain and cloudiness encourage spore release, dispersal, and disease development
other_conditions: Disease severity increases with onset of flowering
Dense planting and closed canopy provide favorable microclimate

disease_development_and_spread: Wind, light rain, and cloudiness encourage spore release and dispersal

cultural_management: Avoid sowing pigeonpea close to bean fields
Rotate crops to reduce chance of pathogen survival

diseases.causal_agent: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (Burkholder) Young, Dye & Wilkie (syn P. phaseolicola)

general: Dark brown angular necrotic spots 1 mm in diameter surrounded by large chlorotic halos 10 mm in diameter on leaves
Spots coalesce under humid conditions giving leaves a blighted appearance
More commonly seen on soft, young leaves of older and ratooned plants
early_symptoms: Dark brown angular necrotic spots 1 mm in diameter with large chlorotic halos 10 mm in diameter
advanced_symptoms: Spots coalesce giving leaves a blighted appearance

field_identification: Dark brown angular necrotic spots with large chlorotic halos

causes_and_risk_factors: More commonly seen on soft, young leaves of older and ratooned plants

favorable_conditions.humidity: Humid conditions cause spots to coalesce; persistent rains and cloudy weather result in severe disease development

general: Appears when plants are flowering as dark gray fungal growths on growing tips, flowers, and pods
Infected flowers drop, reducing pod set
Shed flowers and leaves on the ground covered with sporulating mycelium
advanced_symptoms: Dark gray fungal growths on growing tips, flowers, and pods, flower drop
visual_field_symptoms: Dark gray fungal growth on flowers and pods
Sporulating mycelium on shed flowers and leaves

field_identification: Dark gray fungal growth on flowers, pods, and growing tips during flowering

severity_and_yield_loss: Reduces pod set due to flower drop

diseases.causal_agent: Soil salinity / Accumulation of salts in leaves (Abiotic)

general: Starts with marginal chlorosis and progresses to 'burning' of leaf laminae margins
Commonly observed late in the season
Starts in lower leaves and progresses upwards
advanced_symptoms: Burning of leaf laminae margins progressing upwards
visual_field_symptoms: Margins of leaf laminae showing burnt appearance

field_identification: Marginal chlorosis and burning of leaf margins on lower leaves progressing upwards
differential_diagnosis: Distinguished from fungal leaf blights by systematic nature and absence of chlorotic area between dried and healthy portions of laminae

causes_and_risk_factors: Could be due to soil salinity resulting in gradual accumulation of salts in leaves
Exacerbated by prolonged dry spells

general: Patches of bushy, pale green plants without flowers or pods in the field
Leaves are small and show light and dark green mosaic pattern
Initial mosaic symptoms appear as vein-clearing on young leaves
Infection at 45 days after emergence or later may show symptoms on only some parts while rest appear normal
Some varieties (e.g., ICP 2376) exhibit ring spot leaf symptoms (green islands in chlorotic areas) producing normal flowers and pods
Strains in Bihar (India) and Nepal cause severe internodal shortening, clustering of branches, and filiform leaves
advanced_symptoms: Bushy pale green plants without flowers or pods, small leaves with light/dark green mosaic pattern
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of bushy pale green plants in the field
Infected plants without flowers and pods
Vein clearing symptom on young leaves
Infected leaf with ring spot symptom

field_identification: Patches of bushy, pale green plants lacking flowers/pods
Mosaic pattern, vein-clearing, or ring spot symptoms on small leaves

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: Eriophyid mite Aceria cajani Channabasavanna
Pathogen and mite vector are specific to Cajanus cajan and wild relative C. scarabaeoides var. scarabaeoides
Perennial/volunteer pigeonpeas and ratooned growth provide reservoirs for mite and pathogen

favorable_conditions.temperature: Symptoms suppressed during hot summer months, reappear with monsoon rains
favorable_conditions.humidity: Shade and humidity encourage mite multiplication, especially in hot summer weather
favorable_conditions.rainfall: Monsoon rains bring back symptom expression
other_conditions: High disease incidence when pigeonpeas are inter- or mixed cropped with sorghum or millets

disease_development_and_spread: Transmitted by eriophyid mite Aceria cajani
Mites can be wind-borne up to 2 km from inoculum source
severity_and_yield_loss: A serious problem in Nepal and India, estimated to cause annual pigeonpea grain losses worth US$282 million

cultural_management: Spacing between lines should be maintained at 30 to 40 cms
Weeds should be rouged out at their inception
Maintain timely sowing of the crop
Select a field well away from perennial or ratoon pigeonpeas
Destroy sources of sterility mosaic inoculum, i.e., perennial or ratooned pigeonpeas
Uproot infected plants at an early stage of disease development and destroy them
Rotate crops to reduce sources of inoculum and mite vectors

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: acaricide or insecticides like Kelthane®, Morestan®, metasystox
chemical_management.timing: Early stages of plant growth to control mite vector

general: Green and golden yellow mosaic mottle symptoms on leaves
Sometimes affected parts of leaves become necrotic
Diseased plants usually scattered in field, produce fewer pods than normal when infected early
visual_field_symptoms: Green and golden yellow mosaic mottle symptoms on leaves

field_identification: Green and golden yellow mosaic mottle symptoms on leaves

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: White fly Bemisia tabaci Gennadius
Off-season and isolated sowings suffer more because pigeonpea is not a preferred host of whitefly vectors (feed only when forced by absence of other host plants)

cultural_management: Avoid sowing late to reduce disease severity
Uproot and burn infected plants if disease appears on isolated plants in field

general: Excessive proliferation and clustering of branches with small pale green leaves giving a 'witches' broom' appearance
Plants rarely produce flowers and pods
Flowers, if produced, appear in clusters with elongated pedicels
Whole or part of plant may exhibit symptoms depending on intensity
visual_field_symptoms: Clustering of branches with small pale green leaves

field_identification: Excessive branch proliferation and clustering with small pale green leaves ('witches' broom')

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: Leaf hopper Empoasca sp

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas affected with witches' broom
Pull out and destroy any infected plants to minimize secondary spread of disease
Avoid ratoon cropping

general: Recognized only at flowering
Diseased plants scattered in field, bushy with axillary proliferation of phylloid flowers
Flowers are converted into leafy structures
visual_field_symptoms: Floral proliferation (bushy plants with axillary proliferation of phylloid flowers)

field_identification: Bushy plants with flowers converted into leafy structures (phylloid flowers) at flowering
differential_diagnosis: Differs from witches' broom because in phyllody flowers are converted into leafy structures, whereas in witches' broom there are no flowers

causes_and_risk_factors: Vector: Not known
Seen more frequently in off-season sowings than main-season crops, but incidence still low

cultural_management: Select fields away from perennial pigeonpeas and sesamum

general: Affected plants are stunted with few branches
Produce solitary simple leaves with obtuse tips and long petioles attached to stems, twigs, and floral shoots
Axillary flower buds proliferate into abnormal, clustered inflorescences
Flowers are sessile, small, bunchy, and tightly packed giving inflorescences a knotted appearance
Do not produce normal pods
visual_field_symptoms: Floral proliferation (abnormal clustered inflorescences with knotted appearance)

field_identification: Stunted plants with solitary simple leaves (obtuse tips, long petioles) and clustered inflorescences with sessile, tight, bunchy flowers

diseases.causal_agent: Meloidogyne incognita (Kofoid & White) Chitwood, Meloidogyne javanica (Treub) Chitwood, Meloidogyne arenaria (Neal) Chitwood, Meloidogyne acronea Coetzee

general: Aerial parts show no characteristic symptoms, but reduced plant vigor, delayed flowering (in whole or patches), and leaf yellowing indicate infestation
Root galls (knots) are most characteristic symptom visible with naked eye
Examining roots for egg sacs useful when galls are very small
visual_field_symptoms: Infected plants show stunted growth in the field
Root galls

field_identification: Root galls (knots) on main and lateral roots
Stunted growth and leaf yellowing
diagnostic_methods: Examining roots for the presence of egg sacs when galls are very small

causes_and_risk_factors: Meloidogyne incognita and M. javanica widely distributed in tropical/subtropical climates
Wide host range in extensive soil types; crop damage reflective of sandy soils or sandy patches
Weed hosts help maintain high nematode populations
Combined infestations of M. javanica and M. incognita increase severity
Infection increases severity of Fusarium wilt infection

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy soils or sandy patches within fields

severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses of 8 to 35% reported from Caribbean, Africa, and southeast Asia

cultural_management: Select field with no previous record of nematode infestation
Rotate pigeonpea with wheat to reduce nematode populations
Solarize soil in summer to reduce nematode populations

general: Poor and stunted plants evident 30-45 days after sowing
Minute, pearl-like, white females of H. cajani attached to roots visible with naked eye or hand lens (10x)
Nematode infestation can delay flowering and pod formation for more than a week
visual_field_symptoms: Infected plants show stunted growth in the field
Infected roots with pearl-like female nematodes

field_identification: Minute pearl-like white females attached to roots
diagnostic_methods: Observation of females through hand lens (10x)

causes_and_risk_factors: Host range largely confined to Leguminosae, with Sesamum indicum and Phyllanthus maderaspatensis as non-legume hosts
Widespread in sandy loam soils in northern India and black cotton soils in western and southern India
Lives up to 45 cm deep in soil throughout the year
Infestation enhances aggressiveness of Fusarium udum infection in wilt-susceptible pigeonpeas

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy loam soils in northern India and black cotton soils in western and southern India

epidemiology: Summer fallowing reduces densities of H. cajani by 45% at 0-15 cm but does not affect densities at lower soil depths
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses as high as 30% reported
Initial population density of 3 juveniles cm-3 of soil can cause 25% reduction in plant biomass and yield

cultural_management: Select fields with no previous record of nematode infestation
Rotate crops with sorghum, maize, or pearl millet to reduce nematode populations
Solarize soil in summer to reduce nematode populations

general: Infected plants grow less vigorously than healthy ones with smaller root systems
Egg masses covered with soil found on roots upon uprooting
Roots appear dirty because soil particles adhere to mucilaginous nematode egg sacs and are not easily dislodged by shaking
visual_field_symptoms: Plants stunted due to dirty root disease
Infected roots with egg masses

field_identification: Roots appearing dirty due to soil particles adhering to mucilaginous egg masses not dislodged by shaking
diagnostic_methods: Dipping roots in 0.25% trypan blue and rinsing in water selectively colors nematode egg sacs blue while roots are not stained (identifies reniform nematode without microscope)

causes_and_risk_factors: Attacks many crops in 38 subtropical and tropical countries; extensive host range
Can reduce number of Rhizobium nodules produced
Wilt-susceptible genotypes die prematurely when nematode and wilt fungus are both present

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Sandy and red soils (Alfisols) in western and southern India; variable crop growth in northern India
other_conditions: Damage thresholds range from pre-plant nematode densities of 1.0 to 4.0 cm-3 of soil

disease_development_and_spread: Can survive in absence of host for more than 300 days without losing infectivity
epidemiology: Summer fallowing reduces R. reniformis densities to 70% at 0-15 cm soil depth and 36% at 15-30 cm soil depth
severity_and_yield_loss: Infestation severely affects pigeonpea production in Fiji

cultural_management: Select fields with no previous record of nematode infestation
Rotate crops with rice, maize, or groundnut to reduce nematode populations
Solarize soil in summer to reduce nematode populations

paper_level_notes: The document is ICRISAT Information Bulletin No. 42 (Revised 2012): Handbook of Pigeonpea Diseases.
Provides detailed diagnostic keys and multiple tables for disease resistance sources, cultural practices, and chemical control measures.
